name: Ehueun
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Elugbe, Ben O. 1989. Comparative Edoid: phonology and lexicon (Delta Series 6). Port Harcourt. Covers Ehueun (Edoid); cited on Glottolog ehue1238. Not online.

new_statements.quote: [1989 p.98, 4.19.8 Tone] Elugbe (1973) makes the point that the Ehuẹun system is probably in a fluid transitory stage. Arguing that the system lends itself to a three-level (high, mid, low) analysis as well as to a 'two tone plus downstep' one, Elugbe nonetheless opts for a three-level analysis. [1973 p.279 fn.1] ... as this is a three level tone language, low will be marked even in verb stems to avoid confusion with the unmarked mid. [1973 p.287, 6. Tone] The tones of Ehuẹun do not submit easily to analysis. The whole system is probably in a fluid transitory stage. [1973 p.293] If this analysis be adopted, then Ehuẹun has high, mid, and low tonemes at the tonemic level. [p.295] Even so, the latter analysis is adopted ...

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked in (symlinks resolve to../ghot1243/, both Zenodo CC-BY scans). (1) Elugbe 1989 Comparative Edoid: I re-extracted PDF page 115 (= printed p. 98) directly from with extracted text; sec. 4.19.8 'Tone' reads exactly as quoted: 'Elugbe (1973) makes the point that the Ehuẹun system is probably in a fluid transitory stage. Arguing that the system lends itself to a three-level (high, mid, low) analysis as well as to a 'two tone plus downstep' one, Elugbe nonetheless opts for a three-level analysis.' 4.19.1 gives syllables CV, V; 4.19.9 morphology; nothing on stress. grep over the whole 576 KB text layer of the book: 'stress' 0 hits; 'accent' only once ('heavily accented variety of Yor…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ehueun is described solely as a lexical/grammatical tone language with three level tonemes (high, mid, low; an alternative two-tones-plus-downstep analysis is discussed and rejected); syllables are CV or V; the only suprasegmental section in either description is 'Tone' and no statement about word stress or accent is made.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: noun patterns LH, HL, HH do not occur; LM and MH are in free variation; verbs are not lexically classified by tone; Ukue loans from Yoruba aside, mid is treated as a full third level in Ehueun.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (noun and verb citation forms) and completive noun+noun phrase tonal alternations; no stress domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Elugbe sources describe the Ehuẹun spoken at Epinmi (Ekpinmi, Ekpeme), Akoko, Ondo State = Glottolog ehue1238 exactly; Elugbe 1989 notes it is sometimes lumped with Ukue (ukue1238) but treats them as separate languages with separate sketches (4.19 Ehueun, 4.20 Ukue).

sources.note: Sec. 4.19 Ehueun sketch (pp. 97-98): syllables CV/V, inventories, no vowel harmony; 4.19.8 Tone (p. 98): three-level (H, M, L) analysis vs 'two tone plus downstep', three-level adopted after Elugbe 1973. Nothing on stress or accent; the word 'stress' does not occur in the book.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en), 'Ehueun language' (raw wikitext fetched sources 2026-09-17); cites Archangeli & Pulleyblank 1994 Grounded Phonology p. 181ff (vowels), Mielke 2008 The Emergence of Distinctive Features p. 136ff (inventory), Ladefoged & Maddieson SOWL (rhotics) -- all second-hand from Elugbe.
sources.note: Segment inventory and vowel sets only; nothing on tone or stress.

sources.citation: Elugbe, Ben Ohi. 1989. Edoid. In John Bendor-Samuel (ed.), The Niger-Congo Languages, 291-304. Lanham: University Press of America. [Zenodo 5618102]
sources.note: Lists Ehueun (Ekpenmen, Ekpinmi) in NW Edoid/Osse (p. 296); sec. 13.3.4 Tone systems (p. 299) surveys Edoid tone systems but does not mention Ehueun; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Elugbe, Benny Ohiomamhe. 1973. A comparative Edo phonology. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics and Nigerian Languages, University of Ibadan. [Zenodo 4467456, CC-BY-4.0; scan of Vol. I, 306 pp., image-only]
sources.note: Ehueun phonemic statement pp. 277-296; sec. 6 Tone pp. 287-296: tones 'do not submit easily to analysis', system 'in a fluid transitory stage'; noun patterns LL, LM~MH, ML, MM, HM; weighs two-tones-plus-downstep vs three-level analysis and adopts three levels (H, M, L) (p. 295); p. 279 fn. 1 calls it 'a three level tone language'. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the chapter or in the general Tone section (pp. 90-92).
